72: (2) One who slaughters on Shabbos for a sick person — whether the person became ill before Shabbos or became ill that day — a healthy person is permitted to eat from it raw {on Shabbos.} But one who cooks {or performed another melacha} for a sick person — it is forbidden {on Shabbos} for a healthy person or for a sick person who is not in danger, for we fear he may increase the quantity for him. {Rama: And even if a non-Jew cooked it, it is forbidden on Shabbos (Tosafos, first chapter of Gittin; Ran, chapter Ein Ma'amidin). And if he cut fruits from something attached to the ground for a sick person on Shabbos, even if the person had been ill from before Shabbos, it is forbidden for a healthy person on Shabbos because it grows and increases on Shabbos and there is the concern of muktzeh (Beit Yosef in the name of the Or Zarua).}
75: (4) 'That he became ill today' — and even though the animal was muktzeh on account of the prohibition of slaughtering, nevertheless it is permitted, for we rule like R' Shimon that there is no muktzeh on account of a prohibition except when he set it aside with his own hands, as in a lamp that was lit on Shabbos [Maggid Mishneh chapter 2]. And it is difficult: if so, muktzeh of something attached should also be permitted when the fruits fell — one can answer that there the reason is lest he climb and detach, as stated at the beginning of Beitza — see there for an additional reason in the Beit Yosef.
77: (5) 'Raw on Shabbos' — and without salting [Tur]; see Yoreh De'ah siman 67 seif 2 that rinsing is nonetheless required, and see siman 325 seif 11.
79: (6) 'Lest he increase for him' — this is a Torah-level prohibition when he increases for him, even before placing the pot on the fire. And there are those who say it is rabbinic — see the Beit Yosef.
81: (7) 'And even if he cooked, etc.' — but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately [Shach], and the reason is that since the non-Jew cooked with permission one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu.
83: (8) 'Because it grows and continues growing' — this refers to fruit whose ripening was not yet complete [Beit Yosef]. But when its ripening has been completed we do not say it grows and increases — for otherwise why would we need in the first chapter of Beitza to forbid something attached because lest he climb and detach, or because of muktzeh? See Tosafos in Bava Kamma 69b that what grows is nullified in the majority; see siman 320 seif 2.
85: (4) 'Raw [meat]' — and without salting [Tur]; see Yoreh De'ah siman 67 seif 2 that rinsing is nonetheless required, and see siman 325 seif 11.
87: (5) 'On Shabbos' — but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately. The Shach explains that since the non-Jew cooked with permission one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu, Magen Avraham. And see Yoreh De'ah siman 113, note 10, where I wrote in the name of the later authorities that it is forbidden even to the sick person himself at Motzei Shabbos — see there.
89: (6) 'And it increases' — this refers to fruit whose ripening is not yet complete [Beit Yosef]. But when its ripening has been completed we do not say it grows and increases — Magen Avraham, see there.
91: (5) 'Or performed another melacha' — for the same reason stated regarding slaughtering, where the permission applies specifically because it is impossible to do otherwise.
93: (6) 'Or for a sick person' — the Rashba writes that this too follows the same reason, for regarding melacha performed by a Jew there is no distinction between him and a healthy person.
95: (7) 'And even' — Tosafos in Gittin explain that what is stated in Eruvin 86 — a non-Jew comforted him alongside his mother — only for circumcision did they permit.
97: (8) 'On Shabbos' — to exclude Motzei Shabbos. And there is no issue of bishul akum since it is not common, there is no concern of intermarriage.
99: (9) 'And if, etc., even, etc.' — this is from Chullin there, such as where one cut a gourd. Meaning, even for a sick person who was ill before Shabbos, similar to the first clause regarding slaughtering — unlike Rashi there. And we do not say that the growths are nullified in the majority of the main fruit, because it is a davar she'yesh lo matirin, as Tosafos wrote in Bava Kamma 69a.
101: (10) 'Because it grows, etc.' — this concern does not apply to an animal, and therefore they were not concerned about this. See Tosafos Yom Tov 37b.
103: (2) 'On Shabbos' — see the Beer Heitev there; and in the matter of the vessels, they are customarily instructed to kasher them by hag'alah three times, as explained in Yoreh De'ah there.
105: (8) 'That he became ill today' — we do not say that the animal is muktzeh because of the prohibition of slaughtering, even though the sick person was not yet ill at twilight and the animal was then muktzeh on account of the prohibition of slaughtering. Nevertheless, since the animal was not set aside by hand but was standing ready for slaughter, it is not muktzeh.
107: (9) 'A healthy person is permitted, etc.' — the reason is that since the primary purpose of the slaughtering is for the sick person, and it is impossible to take even a kezayis of meat without slaughtering, there is no concern that he may increase for him.
109: (10) 'It may be eaten raw on Shabbos' — without salting, since salting is forbidden on Shabbos. And rinsing is required because of visible blood. This is not so for blood that is absorbed within the meat, as long as it has not emerged.
111: (11) 'It is forbidden for the sick person' — but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately, and one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu. And tasting whether the dish is good for the sick person is also permitted on Shabbos.
113: (12) 'Whose life is not in danger' — for he too is like a healthy person regarding this matter, for it is forbidden by Torah law to cook for him through a Jew, and we are concerned that if we permit benefit from this they may increase the amount on Shabbos.
115: (13) 'Lest one increase for him' — to put meat into the pot. This is a Torah-level prohibition when one increases for him, even if he adds everything at once before placing the pot on the fire.
117: (14) 'It is forbidden on Shabbos' — for a healthy person to benefit from it, but at Motzei Shabbos it is permitted immediately, and the reason is that since the non-Jew cooked with permission one does not need to wait b'chedi she'ya'asu. Also the Sages did not make a decree regarding benefit from a non-Jew's cooking in this unusual case.
119: (15) 'If he was sick before Shabbos' — in that case there may have been intent before Shabbos to detach the fruit for him if needed. However the prohibition of muktzeh still applies since the fruit is attached.
121: (16) 'And there is the concern of muktzeh' — the later authorities asked about these words of the Rama: why is the small amount that grew on Shabbos not nullified in the main fruit? And it appears to explain that we are dealing with vegetables that grow quickly, such as gourds, and the addition that grew on Shabbos is significant. However a fruit like an orange that was detached on Shabbos for a critically ill person, and the sick person ate a slice from it — it is permitted for a healthy person to eat the rest of the fruit.
123: (8) 'One who slaughters on Shabbos for a sick person' — after the previous seif discussed food cooked on Shabbos in violation of the law, this seif discusses food prepared on Shabbos in a permitted manner due to pikuach nefesh, namely for a critically ill person.
125: (9) 'Whether he became ill that day' — one might have thought that if a sick person was already present before Shabbos, we know that tomorrow we will need to slaughter for him; but when he became ill on Shabbos — we did not know this at the entry of Shabbos, and therefore the meat is muktzeh. However as halacha, an animal standing ready for slaughter has its prohibition removed at the moment it is slaughtered, and it is not muktzeh.
127: (10) 'To eat from it raw' — since no prohibition was done here, for it is permitted to slaughter for a critically ill person, and this slaughtering is sufficient for many people without adding any forbidden melachos.
129: (11) 'Another melacha' — the Rama notes that the law is not limited to cooking. It applies to any melacha that resembles cooking and not slaughtering, in that one who performs it for more than one person must increase its performance.
131: (12) 'Lest he increase for him' — lest he intentionally put more into the pot than is needed for the sick person, so that healthy people can also eat from the leftovers.
133: (13) 'It is forbidden on Shabbos' — if a non-Jew cooked for the sick person there is no concern that a Jew will increase, since the non-Jew is permitted to cook, and the prohibition of benefit from a non-Jew's cooking is only rabbinic. Nevertheless the Sages did not make distinctions in their rulings and forbade it even when the non-Jew cooks. But in such a case, at Motzei Shabbos the food is permitted immediately.
135: (14) 'For a sick person on Shabbos' — fruits attached to a tree at the entry of Shabbos are muktzeh machmas issur, since in order to use them on Shabbos he must transgress the prohibition of detaching, and they are forbidden on Shabbos due to muktzeh even if they were detached in a permitted manner, such as by a non-Jew.
137: (15) 'If he was sick before Shabbos' — and then seemingly the fruits are not muktzeh, since his intention was to detach them on Shabbos if the sick person would need them.
139: (16) 'And there is the concern of muktzeh' — the later authorities asked about these words of the Rama: why is the small amount that grew on Shabbos not nullified in the main fruit? And it appears to explain that we are dealing with vegetables that grow quickly, such as gourds, and the addition that grew on Shabbos is significant. However a fruit like an orange that was detached on Shabbos for a critically ill person, and the sick person ate a slice from it — it is permitted for a healthy person to eat the rest of the fruit.
